subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 1! In this unit you will become an expert on all the numbers from 0 to 100. You use these numbers every single day, even when you do not notice. When Amina counts the goats coming home in the evening, when Yusuf checks that he has 64 pages left in his reading book, or when Halima counts out shillings at the Hargeisa market, they are all using numbers to 100.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 2 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Read, write and represent numbers from 0 to 100.
Say and show the value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens and ones).
Count on and back in ones, twos and tens from any number.
Estimate how many objects there are, then count carefully to check.
Compare two numbers and use the symbols >, < and =.
Put a set of numbers in order from smallest to greatest.
Make and describe number sequences and use ordinal numbers (1st, 2nd, 3rd).
Say and write ordinal numbers from first to twelfth and beyond, including the irregular spellings of fifth, eighth, ninth and twelfth.
Count on from any small number in steps of three and in steps of four.

concepts.title: The 100 Square and Its Patterns
concepts.explanation:
The 100 square is a grid that holds every number from 1 to 100. It has 10 rows and 10 columns, so there are 10 numbers in each row and 10 rows going down. Picture it like the shelves in Omar’s shop, with ten jars on every shelf and ten shelves altogether – one hundred jars in all.

Look carefully and you will spot patterns that make numbers much easier to understand:

Every row starts with a number ending in 1 (1, 11, 21, 31 …).

Every row ends with a number ending in 0 (10, 20, 30, 40 …).

If you move one step to the right, the number goes up by 1.

If you move one step down, the number goes up by 10.

If you move one step up, the number goes down by 10.

These patterns are your friends. If Farah is on 34 and wants to know the number just below it, she does not need to count all the way – she simply adds 10 to get 44. Moving around the 100 square is like walking between houses on a very tidy street where every address follows a rule.

Let us explore a little more. Look down any single column, for example the column that starts with 3: you will read 3, 13, 23, 33, 43, 53, 63, 73, 83, 93. Do you notice that the ones digit never changes – it stays 3 all the way down – while the tens digit climbs by one each row? That is the counting-in-tens pattern hiding inside the grid. Now look along any row, say the row from 41 to 50: the tens digit stays 4 while the ones digit climbs 1, 2, 3, 4 and so on. Seeing both patterns at once is like seeing the bones inside the whole number system.
concepts.example: Here is a small investigation to try. Put your finger on any number, then jump to the number that is one row down and one column to the right. How much bigger is it? (It is 11 bigger, because you added 10 by going down and 1 more by going right.) Patterns like this turn slow counting into quick, confident thinking. The more you play on the 100 square, the more these jumps become automatic.

concepts.title: Place Value – Tens and Ones
concepts.explanation:
This is the big idea of the whole unit. Every two-digit number is built from tens and ones. The digit on the left tells you how many tens. The digit on the right tells you how many ones.

Let us look closely at the number 47:

The 4 is in the tens place, so it stands for 4 tens = 40.

The 7 is in the ones place, so it stands for 7 ones = 7.

We can picture 47 using sticks and dots, the way many teachers show it with real bundles of counting sticks. Each stick bundle is a group of ten; each single dot is one:

Tens: | | | | (4 bundles of ten) Ones: • • • • • • • (7 single dots)

This is why place value matters so much. The digit 4 does not always mean four. In 47 it means forty. In 74 the very same digit 4 means only four ones, and it is the 7 that now means seventy. The position changes the value. If Hassan mixes up the positions and writes 74 when he means 47, he has written a completely different number – he has thirty extra!

Let us look at three more numbers so the idea becomes solid. In 23, the 2 is worth 2 tens = 20 and the 3 is worth 3 ones = 3, so 23 = 20 + 3. In 90, the 9 is worth 9 tens = 90 and the 0 tells us there are no ones, so 90 = 90 + 0. And in a single-digit number like 8, there are no tens at all – just 8 ones. Notice how the zero in 90 is doing an important job: it holds the ones place empty so the 9 stays in the tens place. Without that zero, 90 would collapse into 9. We call a zero used this way a place holder.
concepts.example: A good way to feel place value in your hands is to think of bundled counting sticks, just as Sagal does when she helps at Nuur Academy. A loose stick is one. Ten sticks tied together is one ten. To build 34, she lays down 3 bundles and 4 loose sticks. To build 43, she lays down 4 bundles and 3 loose sticks. The same digits, but a very different pile of sticks – because the places have swapped. Try this yourself with stones or beans and you will never forget what place value means.

concepts.title: Different Ways to Show a Number
concepts.explanation:
One number can wear many different clothes. Take the number 36. We can show it as:

As a picture: | | | • • • • • • (3 sticks and 6 dots)

On a number line: a point between 30 and 40, closer to 40

As a part-whole model: 36 splits into 30 and 6

Being able to move between these different pictures is a sign that you really understand a number. When Khadija sees 36 written in words, in dots, and on a number line, and knows they are all the same, she truly owns that number.

The part-whole model deserves a closer look because you will use it again and again. It shows a number split into its parts. The whole number 36 sits at the top, and its two parts – 30 and 6 – hang below it like two branches of a tree. This picture reminds us that 36 is really 30 and 6 joined together. Later, when you learn to add and subtract, the part-whole model will help you see how numbers come apart and fit back together. For now, practise splitting numbers into their tens and ones part: 58 splits into 50 and 8; 71 splits into 70 and 1; 40 splits into 40 and 0.
concepts.example: The number line is another picture worth mastering. Imagine the road from Mogadishu to the next town, with a marker every ten kilometres: 0, 10, 20, 30, all the way to 100. Each number has its own place on this road. Numbers on the left are smaller, numbers on the right are larger. To place 36, you find the stretch between 30 and 40 and make your mark a little past the middle, because 36 is closer to 40 than to 30. The number line helps you *see* how big a number is and how far apart two numbers are.

concepts.title: Counting in Ones, Twos and Tens
concepts.explanation:
Counting one at a time is fine for small groups, but slow for large ones. Imagine Idris counting 60 dates one by one – he would soon lose his place. Smarter counting saves time.

Counting in ones: 41, 42, 43, 44, 45 … The ones digit changes each time; the tens digit stays the same until you pass a ten.

Counting in twos: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 … These are the even numbers. The numbers you skip (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) are the odd numbers.

Counting in tens: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 … The ones digit stays the same (a 0), and the tens digit goes up by one each time. This is the fastest way to count large groups. Zahra counts a big pile of goats’ milk cups by making rings of ten first, then counting 10, 20, 30, 40.

You can also count in tens starting from a number that is not a ten. For example, start at 4 and count on in tens: 4, 14, 24, 34, 44. Notice the ones digit stays 4 the whole way. This is a powerful shortcut. If Ibrahim has 24 sweets and his mother gives him another ten, he does not count one by one – he jumps straight to 34. Counting backwards in tens works the same way: from 90 you go 90, 80, 70, 60, 50, taking away ten each time.
concepts.example: It is also important to know odd and even numbers well. Even numbers can be shared into two equal groups with nothing left over – they end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Odd numbers always have one left over when you try to share them into two – they end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. When Maryam shares 8 dates between two friends, each gets 4 with none left over, so 8 is even. When she tries to share 7 dates equally, one date is always left over, so 7 is odd. You can spot whether any number is odd or even just by looking at its last digit – a very handy trick.

concepts.title: Estimating Then Counting
concepts.explanation:
An estimate is a sensible guess made before you count carefully. It is not a wild number pulled from the air – it is a thoughtful guess based on what you can see. Estimating first is a habit good mathematicians keep for the rest of their lives, because it warns you if your final count goes badly wrong.

Suppose Omar tips a bag of dates onto a mat. Before counting, he glances and thinks, ‘That looks like about 30.’ Then he groups them into rings of ten and counts: 10, 20, 30, and 3 left over – 33 dates. His estimate of 30 was close, so he can trust his count. But imagine he had counted and got 83; the huge gap from his estimate of 30 would tell him to stop and count again, because something went wrong.
concepts.example: How do you make a good estimate? Look at a small group you can count quickly – say ten objects – and picture how many of those groups would fill the whole pile. If the pile looks like about four of those groups, estimate 40. The more you practise, the sharper your estimates become. Estimating and counting work together like two hands: one guesses, the other checks.

concepts.title: Comparing and Ordering Numbers
concepts.explanation:
To compare two numbers means to decide which is greater, which is smaller, or whether they are equal. The trick is to use place value:

First look at the tens digit. The number with more tens is greater.

If the tens are the same, then look at the ones digit to decide.

Compare 47 and 32: 47 has 4 tens, 32 has 3 tens. Since 4 tens is more than 3 tens, 47 > 32. We did not even need to look at the ones.

Compare 63 and 68: both have 6 tens, so we look at the ones. 63 has 3 ones, 68 has 8 ones, and 8 is more than 3, so 68 > 63.

We write comparisons using three symbols. A helpful trick: the open, hungry mouth of the symbol always points at the bigger number, like a crocodile that wants the larger meal.

To order a set of numbers means to line them up, usually from smallest to greatest. Look at the tens first, and use the ones to break any ties. This is exactly what a shopkeeper does when arranging price tags from cheapest to most expensive. Here is a careful method: find the smallest number and write it down, cross it off your list, then find the smallest of what remains, and repeat until every number is placed. For 38, 83, 56, 29, 72 you would pick 29 first, then 38, then 56, then 72, then 83.
concepts.example: A word of warning that catches many learners: a number is not bigger just because it has a bigger ones digit. Compare 49 and 51. The 9 in 49 is large, but 49 has only 4 tens while 51 has 5 tens, so 51 is the greater number. Always let the tens speak first. This is why Zara’s idea – ‘just look at the tens to order numbers’ – is only *sometimes* true: it works when the tens are different, but when two numbers share the same tens you must look at the ones to decide.

concepts.title: Ordinal Numbers – First to Tenth and Beyond
concepts.explanation: Ordinal numbers tell us the position of something in a line or order — not how many there are, but where something comes: first, second, third, and so on. You already know the first three: 1st is first, 2nd is second, 3rd is third. These three are special because their words do not follow a simple pattern, so you must learn them by heart. After third, most ordinal numbers follow a friendly pattern: just add the letters '-th' to the counting number. 4 becomes 4th (fourth), 6 becomes 6th (sixth), 7 becomes 7th (seventh), 10 becomes 10th (tenth). But watch out for a few words that change their spelling a little: five becomes 5th (fifth, not fiveth), eight becomes 8th (eighth, only one t), and nine becomes 9th (ninth, no e). Once you reach ten, the pattern keeps going: 11th is eleventh, 12th is twelfth (notice the spelling change again), and 20th is twentieth.
concepts.example: Here is the full list from first to twelfth, so you can check yourself any time: 1st first, 2nd second, 3rd third, 4th fourth, 5th fifth, 6th sixth, 7th seventh, 8th eighth, 9th ninth, 10th tenth, 11th eleventh, 12th twelfth. At the Nuur Academy sports day, if Halima finishes 5th and Omar finishes 9th, Omar crossed the line four places behind Halima.

concepts.title: Counting On in Threes and Fours
concepts.explanation: You already know how to count on in twos and tens. Counting in threes and fours works exactly the same way, except each jump is a little bigger. To count on in threes, start at any number and keep adding 3. Starting at 0: 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18… each number is 3 more than the last. Starting from a different number works the same way — starting at 2 and counting on in threes gives 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17… To count on in fours, start at any number and keep adding 4. Starting at 0: 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24… Starting at 1 and counting on in fours gives 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21…
concepts.example: Counting in threes is useful for sharing into groups of three, like when Yusuf lines up camels in rows of three: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 camels for 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 rows. Counting in fours is useful for counting legs on animals such as goats: 1 goat has 4 legs, 2 goats have 4 + 4 = 8 legs, 3 goats have 8 + 4 = 12 legs.

methods.title: How to compare two numbers
steps: Look at the tens digit of each number.
If one has more tens, that number is greater — stop.
If the tens are the same, compare the ones digits.
Write the correct symbol: >, < or =.

methods.title: How to count a large collection
methods.example: In the number 85, what is the value of the 8?
steps: Estimate first — make a sensible guess.
Group the objects into rings of ten.
Count the tens: 10, 20, 30 …
Count the leftover ones and add them on.

methods.title: Find the rule: how does each number change?
methods.example: Sagal has a basket of mangoes. She makes rings of ten and has 4 full rings and 6 left over. How many mangoes?
steps: Check the rule works between two or three pairs.
Apply the rule again and again to fill the gaps.
Check your rule against every pair in the sequence — if one does not fit, look again for a different pattern.

methods.title: Compare two numbers
steps: 75 has 7 tens; 57 has 5 tens.
Since 7 tens is more than 5 tens, 75 > 57.
The crocodile mouth opens towards 75.

methods.title: Continue a sequence
methods.example: A sequence starts at 37 and counts on in tens, stopping at 77. Write it out.
steps: Add ten each time: 37, 47, 57, 67, 77.
Notice the ones digit stays 7 the whole way, and the tens digit climbs by one each step.
Check your sequence follows the same rule (add ten) all the way to the end.

methods.title: Order a set of numbers
methods.example: Put these camel counts in order from smallest to greatest: 67, 42, 86, 34, 21.
steps: Compare the tens first.
The tens digits are 6, 4, 8, 3 and 2.
Order those from smallest: 21 (2 tens), 34 (3 tens), 42 (4 tens), 67 (6 tens), 86 (8 tens).
None of the tens are equal here, so we do not even need the ones.

workedExamples.title: Fill the gaps in a row
workedExamples.solution: This row counts on in ones. After 22 comes 23. After 24 comes 25. So the row is 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26. The ones digit goes up by one each step while the tens digit stays as 2.

workedExamples.title: Show the value of a digit
workedExamples.prompt: In the number 85, what is the value of the 8?
workedExamples.solution: The 8 sits in the tens place, so it is worth 8 tens = 80. The 5 is worth 5 ones. So 85 = 80 + 5.

workedExamples.title: Count a collection the smart way
workedExamples.prompt: Sagal has a basket of mangoes. She makes rings of ten and has 4 full rings and 6 left over. How many mangoes?
workedExamples.solution: 4 rings of ten = 40. Then add the 6 ones. 40 + 6 = 46 mangoes. Counting in tens first made this quick and safe.

workedExamples.title: Compare two numbers
workedExamples.solution: 75 has 7 tens; 57 has 5 tens. Since 7 tens is more than 5 tens, 75 > 57. The crocodile mouth opens towards 75.

workedExamples.title: Continue a sequence
workedExamples.prompt: A sequence starts at 37 and counts on in tens, stopping at 77. Write it out.
workedExamples.solution: Add ten each time: 37, 47, 57, 67, 77. Notice the ones digit stays 7 the whole way, and the tens digit climbs by one each step.

workedExamples.title: Order a set of numbers
workedExamples.prompt: Put these camel counts in order from smallest to greatest: 67, 42, 86, 34, 21.
workedExamples.solution: Compare the tens first. The tens digits are 6, 4, 8, 3 and 2. Order those from smallest: 21 (2 tens), 34 (3 tens), 42 (4 tens), 67 (6 tens), 86 (8 tens). None of the tens are equal here, so we do not even need the ones. The order is 21, 34, 42, 67, 86.

workedExamples.title: An ordinal problem
workedExamples.prompt: Abdi is 4th in the line for water. The two people at the very front fill their buckets and leave. What position is Abdi in now?
workedExamples.solution: Two people left from the front, so everyone behind them moves up by two places. Abdi was 4th, so he becomes 4 − 2 = 2nd. If those two people had joined the back of the line instead, Abdi would still be 4th.

workedExamples.title: Make the smallest odd number
workedExamples.prompt: Using the digit cards 3, 5, 7 and 9, make the smallest possible odd two-digit number.
workedExamples.solution: To make a number small, put the smallest digit in the tens place, because tens count for the most. The smallest card is 3, so the tens digit is 3. To make it odd, the ones digit must be odd — and all the remaining cards (5, 7, 9) are odd, so choose the smallest of them, which is 5. The answer is 35.

workedExamples.title: What is the value of the underlined digit
workedExamples.prompt: What is the value of the underlined digit? a) 7 in 7͟3 b) 5 in 5͟8.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: Using digit cards 2, 4, 6 and 8, make the largest possible even two-digit number and the smallest possible even two-digit number.
workedExamples.solution: 1) Largest even = 86; smallest even = 24 (0 is not among the cards, so use 2 in the tens and 4 in the ones).

activities.title: Make Your Own 100 Square
steps: Draw a grid with 10 boxes across and 10 boxes down.
Write the numbers 1 to 100, ten in each row.
Colour every number you say when counting in tens.
Colour the even numbers in a second colour. What pattern do you see?
Keep your 100 square – you can use it all through this unit as your number map.

activities.title: Bundles of Ten (Place-Value Sticks)
activities.materials: 47 small sticks, stones, or dry beans, and some string or rubber bands.
steps: Count out your objects and tie them into bundles of ten.
Count how many full bundles (tens) and how many are left over (ones).
Say the number: ‘___ tens and ___ ones make ___.’
Ask a family member to call out a number under 100 and build it with bundles and singles.

activities.title: The Crocodile Compare Game
activities.materials: paper number cards from 0 to 99 (write them yourself).
steps: Shuffle the cards and place them face down.
Each player turns over one card.
Draw a crocodile mouth (> or <) pointing at the greater number.
The player with the greater number keeps both cards. Play until the cards run out.
This game trains you to compare tens first, then ones – fast!

activities.title: Market Counting Investigation
activities.materials: a real or pretend market with items to count (dates, stones as ‘shillings’).
steps: Set out a pile of ‘goods’ and estimate how many there are.
Count them by making rings of ten, then counting in tens and ones.
Compare your estimate to the real count. How close were you?
Do it three times and see if your estimates get better.

activities.title: Ordinal Line-Up (Family Game)
steps: Line up five or more people.
Call out ordinals: ‘The 3rd person, hop!’ ‘The 1st person, clap!’
Now have someone leave the front. Ask everyone their new position.
Talk about how positions change when people join or leave.

activities.title: Number Sequence Snake
steps: Draw a long snake and divide its body into boxes.
Choose a starting number and a rule (for example, start at 20, count on in fives... or tens).
Fill the snake with your sequence.
Give a friend a snake with gaps and let them fill in the missing numbers.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand tens and ones best? What was the trickiest part? What would you like more practice with? Share your answer with your teacher at your next session, or with your AI tutor right away if your teacher is not available.

rules.title: Place Value Rule
rules.text: Left digit = tens. Right digit = ones. 47 = 4 tens + 7 ones = 40 + 7.

rules.title: Comparing Rule
rules.text: Compare the tens first. More tens = greater number. If the tens are equal, compare the ones. The open mouth of > or < always points at the bigger number.

rules.title: Odd and Even Rule
rules.text: Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A sequence starts at 42, counts on in tens, and stops at 92. Write every number.
Zara says, ‘You only need to look at the tens to order numbers.’ Is this always, sometimes, or never true? Explain with an example.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Sometimes true – it works when the tens differ, like comparing 72 and 45 (7 tens beats 4 tens, so no need to check the ones). But when the tens are equal, you must also check the ones, like comparing 63 and 68 (both have 6 tens, so you look at the ones: 3 is less than 8, so 63 is smaller).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Waris is 2nd in line and 3 people join behind her. What position is she in now? Why?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Waris stays 2nd. The 3 people join behind her, further back in the line, so nobody in front of her changes. Only people joining or leaving in front of a person can change that person's position.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Estimating Then Counting.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
An estimate is a sensible guess made before you count carefully. It is not a wild number pulled from the air – it is a thoughtful guess based on what you can see. Estimating first is a habit good mathematicians keep for the rest of their lives, because it warns you if your final count goes badly wrong.

Suppose Omar tips a bag of dates onto a mat. Before counting, he glances and thinks, ‘That looks like about 30.’ Then he groups them into rings of ten and counts: 10, 20, 30, and 3 left over – 33 dates. His estimate of 30 was close, so he can trust his count. But imagine he had counted and got 83; the huge gap from his estimate of 30 would tell him to stop and count again, because something went wrong.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Comparing and Ordering Numbers.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: To compare two numbers means to decide which is greater, which is smaller, or whether they are equal. The trick is to use place value: First look at the tens digit. The number with more tens is greater.

selfAssessment: I can this unit is designed for self-paced learning. That means you move at your own speed. Read each explanation slowly, try every worked example yourself on paper, and only move on when you feel ready. Your AI tutor is available day and night to give you extra practice, explain a step in a new way, or check your answers. Your teacher will also meet with you about twice a week to help with anything that feels tricky.

I can why does this matter so much? Numbers are the language of the world around you. Traders in the market use them to give the right change. Farmers use them to count livestock and know if any goat is missing. Families use them to share food fairly at iftar during Ramadan. Even the prayer times follow numbers. When you become confident with numbers to 100, you are gaining a skill you will use every day for the rest of your life – and you are building the strong foundation you need for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing in the units to come.

I can as you work, keep a pencil and some paper beside you. Mathematics is not a subject you can learn only by reading – you must do it. Draw the pictures, write the numbers, and say the answers out loud. If you get something wrong, that is not a failure; it is simply a sign of exactly what to practise next. Every mathematician you admire once sat where you sit now, learning these very same ideas.
I can read, write and represent numbers from 0 to 100.
I can say and show the value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens and ones).
I can count on and back in ones, twos and tens from any number.
I can estimate how many objects there are, then count carefully to check.
I can compare two numbers and use the symbols >, < and =.
